title: Snake Tongues Sample 100x More Air. Why Do They Flick? 🐍
description:
Why do snakes flick their forked tongues? The tongue collects scent particles for the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth, and its two tips let a snake smell in stereo.

topic: Why do snakes flick their forked tongues?
script: A snake's tongue can't taste a thing, so why do you see it flick nonstop? Because it's a scent collector. Each flick grabs tiny particles, from the air and the ground. It pulls back in, and drops them inside the mouth. From there, they reach a special organ, in the roof of the mouth. That's where the smelling happens. Now look at the fork. The two tips spread apart, up to twice as wide as its head. So each tip samples a different spot, like your two ears. If the left tip smells stronger, dinner went left. That's smelling in stereo. In the air, the flicking tongue whips up tiny swirls, that pull smells in, sampling a hundred times more air, than a simple dip. If your tongue could smell, what would you follow first?
key_facts: The tongue has no taste or smell receptors; those are in the vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the roof of the mouth (Live Science)

Chemicals are deposited inside the mouth and reach the organ; X-ray work points to floor-of-mouth pads, Schwenk describes tip-to-organ delivery, so the script says only 'inside the mouth' then 'reach'
Tips can spread up to twice the head's width (Live Science)
Each tip compares sides so the brain senses which is stronger (Schwenk, Britannica)
Oscillating flicks create vortices and sample 100 times as much air as a simple downward extension (Live Science)
